Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on February 5, 2025
Review Body:
The Franke family were You Tube famous for the Vlog ‘8 Passengers’ written by mom, Ruby. The vlog ran from 2015 to 2020. Ruby then partnered with Jodi Hilderbrandt to run a ‘parenting’ channel. Both were arrested in 2023 and sentenced to prison in 2024 for aggregated child abuse. This book is written by Shari, the Franke’s eldest daughter, and focuses on her journey and her point of view. She does not speak for her siblings.

Listening to this was hard, frustrating and sad all at the same time. Story is read by Shari Franke, who at times seemed detached and unemotional, monotone. But, after what this poor young women went thru this is totally understandable. I appreciated her candor, leaving nothing out. It was hard because of all the people (father, church bishops) who should have protected her, failed her numerous times by manipulating and grooming her. Frustrating because no one would listen to this child. I wanted to shake them. Sad because this didn’t have to happen. Shari is now a young women who has taken control of her life, healing and learning to build a happy life. This book is about surviving, overcoming and facing forward. I’m happy that Shari has found her voice and is healing. Trigger warning: mental health issues, child abuse.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 24, 2025
Review Body:
This was a deeply moving memoir that captures the emotional turmoil and resilience of a family facing significant challenges. I felt a profound connection with the characters, particularly with the oldest daughter, Shari. Her determination and strength resonated throughout the narrative, making her journey relatable and inspiring.

The emotional weight of the family's experiences is palpable, and I wanted to reach out to each child for what they endured. The fact that this is a true story adds another layer of poignancy, drawing me into a world that felt both heartbreaking and hopeful. Being able to read this in one sitting is a testament to how good it was.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 20, 2025
Review Body:
Devastating. 

Read this for a book club. It's not something I ever would have picked up on my own, because like Shari expresses, I find true crime media to be exploitative. I hope that writing this is healing for Shari and that she doesn't look back and regret it in the future--I worry because she's still so young and because this kind of exploitation is all she's ever known, that she feels compelled to lay all of this bare in a way she wouldn't otherwise. 

The book was well-written, though it could be a bit word-vomity at times, which I completely understand. I switched back and forth between the e-book and the audiobook, and have to say that I'm impressed with Shari's narration. She does an excellent job.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 14, 2025
Review Body: Shari Frankie’s insight into the effects of parental abuse are remarkable, especially for such a young woman. Without a shred of self-pity, Shari describes the pain and hopelessness children feel when dealing with a narcissistic or perfectionist mother. I believe this book will help other survivors of parental abuse put words to their experience. And perhaps it will aid in healing from that abuse as well. Shari relates her steps to self-healing that are uplifting and hope filled.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 11, 2025
Review Body:
Setting aside the horrors of 8 Passengers for a moment, this book was incredibly well written, immediately immersive, and led to quite a bit of self-examination. Shari’s willingness to share the gritty details of her intense therapy work was inspiring and motivating, a gentle nudge that tells us we can all — always — be better versions of ourselves with hard work and uncomfortable truths. Shari’s journey is a testament to the power of introspection, defiance in the face of injustice, and a reminder that no trauma is “too big” to heal from. Thank you for that, Shari, and for your courage to question authority and seek truth even (and especially) when faced with pushback.

As for the 8 Passengers story that was and is so vital to who Shari is — Shari has successfully taken back control of the narrative of her life. I particularly appreciate her protection of her siblings.

Her literary background and years of journaling are apparent in her prose, which still reflects so much of who Shari is — once a relatable teenager, often very witty, so deeply compassionate and empathetic, and most importantly, uncensored. This is Shari’s story, from start to finish, and it’s well worth the read.
